title: Philosophy, Logic and Human Existence
description: The General Studies course in philosophy and logic: the meaning, methods and branches of philosophy, philosophical problems and basic concepts, ethics and ethical theories, the nature of logic and arguments, validity and rules of inference, formal fallacies and syllogisms, and informal fallacies and the uses of language. Built from the University of Ibadan textbook Philosophy, Logic and Critical Thinking (eds. C. O. Agulanna and A. P. Ipadeola).

topics.title: Meaning, Methods and Branches of Philosophy
topics.summary: Philosophy, from the Greek philos (love) and sophia (wisdom), is the love of wisdom pursued through reasoning. It has no single definition, uses methods such as criticism, argumentation, methodic doubt, dialectic and analysis, raises first- and second-order questions, and has four main branches: epistemology, metaphysics, logic and ethics (value theory).
subtopics: Myths and the meaning of philosophy

topics.title: Philosophical Problems and Basic Concepts
topics.summary: Philosophical problems are perennial because they lack generally accepted solutions. In epistemology the main challenge is scepticism; in metaphysics, the problem of universals, materialism and idealism, and the mind-body problem. Concepts are ideas or notions that may be concrete or abstract, relative or non-relative, positive or negative, and collective or non-collective.
subtopics: Universals, realism and nominalism; mind and body

topics.title: Ethics and Ethical Theories
topics.summary: Ethics is an inquiry into the nature of morality and the good life. The classical cardinal virtues are temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice. Ethical theories are deontological (duty-based), consequentialist (utilitarianism, egoism, altruism), virtue ethics, hedonism, relativism and situation ethics, and applied ethics addresses moral dilemmas.
subtopics: Virtue ethics, hedonism, relativism and situation ethics

topics.title: The Nature of Logic and Arguments
topics.summary: Logic is the study of the laws of reasoning, concerned with distinguishing correct from incorrect reasoning. It rests on the laws of identity, contradiction and excluded middle, and divides into informal and formal logic. An argument has premises and a conclusion, marked by indicator words, and is either deductive or inductive.

topics.title: Validity, Soundness and Rules of Inference
topics.summary: Truth and falsity belong to statements; validity belongs to deductive arguments. A valid argument is one whose premises logically imply its conclusion, a matter of form, and a sound argument is valid with true premises. Valid argument forms include modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism and constructive and destructive dilemmas.
subtopics: Validity as a matter of form
Modus ponens, modus tollens and hypothetical syllogism

topics.title: Categorical Syllogisms and Formal Fallacies
topics.summary: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that may seem correct but is not. Formal fallacies violate the rules of valid inference. A categorical syllogism has three terms (major, minor and middle) in two premises and a conclusion, and its validity depends on rules whose violation gives fallacies such as four terms, undistributed middle and illicit major or minor.
subtopics: The categorical syllogism and its terms
Standard form and refutation by analogy

topics.title: Informal Fallacies and the Uses of Language
topics.summary: Informal fallacies come from carelessness or the wish to trick others, and divide into fallacies of relevance and of ambiguity: appeals to force, the person, ignorance, pity, the people and authority, accident and hasty generalisation. Language has informative, expressive and directive functions, and clear use of language aids straight thinking.
subtopics: Appeal to force and to the person
Appeal to ignorance and to pity
Appeal to the people and to authority
